newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba presses attack on Bonn's gold scheme.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba presses attack on Bonn's gold scheme.

text.p: The Bundesbank pressed home its attack on the government's plan to revalue the central bank's official reserves on Monday amid growing uncertainty about the future of European monetary union (EMU).

Three Bundesbank council members, speaking at a reception hosted by a state central bank, criticised the government for seeking to revalue German gold and currency reserves to help it meet EMU criteria and suggested the single currency project was entering a decisive stage.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl, however, defended the asset plan, saying Bundesbank arguments against it were unfounded and that he was ready for reasonable talks with the central bank.

At issue is a scheme put forward by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel more than two weeks ago to revalue the Bundesbank's assets at higher levels, enabling Bonn to use the resulting proceeds to help cut its budgetary deficits.

In a rare public fight with Bonn, the Bundesbank last week rejected the proposal as an attack on its independence and a move that would threaten the stability of the future European currency, the euro.

"Let me state here, clearly and categorically: in no way does the revaluation of the Bundesbank reserves amount to an infringement of the independence of the Bundesbank," Kohl said at an economic conference in Switzerland.
Bundesbank officials are unlikely to be won over by such statements and worried openly about the future of the euro.
Council member Edgar Meister said the monetary union project may enter "rougher waters" in the weeks and months ahead and warned that Germany must not lose its role as guardian of monetary stability.

Meister added the French election outcome on Sunday, which saw the Socialist-led left win a resounding victory, had changed the environment for Europe's planned monetary union and said it may become clear in the next few weeks whether the euro will be a stable currency.
"Since yesterday the constellation has been altered so that we might know in the next few weeks, not in 1998, whether the euro will be a stable currency," Meister said.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick added he did not at present think European monetary union would be postponed but added that he thought a delay would be considered.
"For the time being I don't think they will change the calendar but I think they will think it over," Koebnick told reporters.
Speaking at the same event, Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum stressed there had been no change in the Bundesbank's position since it released a statement last Wednesday.
He added, however, the statement included elements of a potential compromise, but was also very clear in its position in confronting the government's plan.
Gaddum said it was now up to the parliament to decide the outcome of the revaluation debate, but declined to say what that outcome might be.
The Bundesbank's reluctance to sign on to Bonn's revaluation scheme, meanwhile, won the support of a prominent government economic advisor.

Horst Siebert, president of the Kiel Institute fuer Weltwirtschaft (IFW), one of Germany's leading economic institutes, told the Handelsblatt newspaper that he agreed with the Bundesbank that forcing through the revaluation would hurt its independence.
This could also hurt the European Central Bank as the Bundesbank was a particular role model for the future European monetary policy-making group, he said.
